historical_timeline.summary: Formal debut at Wigmore Hall, London, at 16, after the Suggia Award and the Queen's Prize.
Loses sensitivity in her fingers; returns to England exhausted and takes a sabbatical; the numbness worsens on her return to the stage in 1972.
Last public concerts, in London and New York.
Diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in London at 28; her performing career ends.
Appointed OBE; teaches and gives master classes, and raises funds for MS research.
Dies of multiple sclerosis in London at 42.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recognize multiple sclerosis in a professional musician of 28 whose numbness and clumsiness of the fingers and fatigue could be put down to overwork or stress, as hers were for years, and care for it on the AAN 2018 disease-modifying therapy guideline, the ECTRIMS/EAN 2018 guideline and NICE NG220: urgent MRI of the brain and spine with gadolinium; diagnosis by the 2017 McDonald criteria (and their 2024 revision), with cerebrospinal fluid oligoclonal bands and exclusion of mimics (vitamin B12, thyroid, aquaporin-4 antibody for a myelitis; MOG antibody only when the picture suggests it); high-dose corticosteroids for a disabling relapse; early high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy, choosing among ocrelizumab, ofatumumab and natalizumab with JCV antibody status, infusion logistics and pregnancy plans; hepatitis B screening, immunoglobulins and vaccinations before B-cell therapy; vitamin D; infection and pseudo-relapse; fatigue; hand function with occupational therapy; and a plan built around her playing and teaching, set against the four years it took to name her illness in the 1970s, when no disease-modifying treatment existed.

visit_schedule.purpose: Three weeks of numbness and clumsiness in the fingers of both hands, with Lhermitte's sign and fatigue, in a professional cellist of 28: examination, blood tests, and urgent MRI of the brain and spine
Diagnosis of relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis: neurology consultation, treatment of the relapse, choice of high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy, and vaccinations before B-cell therapy
Second half-dose of the first ocrelizumab course: recovery of hand function, infusion reactions, vaccination, practice and work
Same-day sick visit for cystitis with a pseudo-relapse
Three months on ocrelizumab: re-baseline MRI, B-cell depletion, fatigue, vitamin D and hand function
Periodic adult preventive visit on B-cell therapy
Six months: first 600 mg dose of ocrelizumab, no evidence of disease activity, immunoglobulins, vaccination response, pregnancy planning and her return to performing

hpi.narrative: Ms. du Pré returns two weeks after her first visit. MRI of the brain and spine three days after that visit showed lesions typical of multiple sclerosis in the brain and the spinal cord, including an enhancing lesion at C3 to C4 that explains her hands, and the lumbar puncture a week ago showed oligoclonal bands in the spinal fluid only. Aquaporin-4 antibody was negative. She was seen today by Dr. Lindgren-Achebe. The numbness and clumsiness in her fingers are no better; she has practiced for only a few minutes at a time this week and has cancelled two more concerts. The electric feeling down her back when she bends her head continues. She is tired by mid-afternoon. She asked what multiple sclerosis will mean for her playing, and whether she can still have children.

assessment_plan.assessment: Multiple sclerosis by the 2017 McDonald criteria: a current attack (partial cervical myelitis) with an earlier sensory episode in the history, dissemination in space (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord lesions) and in time (enhancing and non-enhancing lesions together), with CSF-specific oligoclonal bands. The 2024 revision is also met, and most lesions show a central vein. Mimics were excluded: vitamin B12 and TSH were normal, aquaporin-4 antibody was negative, and HIV and syphilis serology were negative. MOG antibody was not tested, because nothing suggests MOG antibody disease (no optic neuritis, no long cord lesion, no ADEM-like picture). The relapse limits her hand function and her work, so high-dose steroids are offered. With active disease at 28, Dr. Lindgren-Achebe and she chose early high-efficacy therapy: ocrelizumab, over natalizumab because her JCV antibody is positive (index 1.4) with a higher risk of PML after two years, and over ofatumumab because she prefers two infusions a year to monthly injections when she travels

consultant_note.history: Ms. du Pré, 28, is seen at the request of Dr. Thackeray-Osei two weeks after she presented with numbness and clumsiness of the fingers of both hands, Lhermitte's sign and fatigue. She has since had MRI of the brain and spine with gadolinium and a lumbar puncture. Her fingers are no better: she can practice only a few minutes at a time and has cancelled two more concerts. She recalls a month of finger tingling about 18 months ago that settled without treatment; she has had no visual loss, double vision, imbalance or bladder symptoms. She travels for concerts and teaches. She is not planning a pregnancy this year but would like children in future
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Thackeray-Osei's intake note and results. MRI of the brain with gadolinium: eleven ovoid T2 lesions, eight periventricular (several perpendicular to the ventricles), two juxtacortical and one in the right middle cerebellar peduncle; one periventricular lesion enhances; central veins in most lesions. MRI of the cervical and thoracic spine: short dorsal lesion at C3 to C4 with patchy enhancement, non-enhancing lesion at T7, no swelling. Lumbar puncture: white cells 6, protein 42 mg/dL, six CSF-specific oligoclonal bands, IgG index 0.86. Serum aquaporin-4 IgG (cell-based) negative; HIV and syphilis negative; JCV antibody positive, index 1.4. Vitamin B12 468 pg/mL and TSH 1.6 mIU/L at the first visit. Drawn with the lumbar puncture: hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody negative, surface antibody negative; varicella IgG positive. Today: 25-hydroxyvitamin D 16 ng/mL; IgG 1080 and IgM 124 mg/dL; urine pregnancy test negative

assessment.assessment: Multiple sclerosis by the 2017 McDonald criteria: a current attack of partial cervical myelitis, with dissemination in space in four regions and dissemination in time shown by enhancing and non-enhancing lesions on the same scan; CSF-specific oligoclonal bands add certainty. The 2024 revision is also met, and central veins support the diagnosis. The earlier episode of finger tingling was probably a first attack. Mimics were considered and excluded: normal B12 and thyroid function, negative aquaporin-4 antibody (a cell-based assay is needed for any myelitis), negative HIV and syphilis serology. MOG antibody testing is not indicated: there is no optic neuritis, long cord lesion or ADEM-like illness, and the lesions are typical of MS. With a disabling relapse, an enhancing cord lesion and multiple lesions at 28, her disease is active, and early high-efficacy treatment gives the best long-term outcome
Correct the deficiency; vitamin D is not a treatment for MS

recommendations: Treat the relapse, which limits her hand function and her work: methylprednisolone 1 g intravenously daily for 3 days after a negative urine dipstick (oral methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 5 days is an equivalent alternative)

Early high-efficacy disease-modifying therapy with ocrelizumab: 300 mg intravenously on day 1 and day 15, then 600 mg every six months, with methylprednisolone 100 mg, an antihistamine and acetaminophen before each infusion. Natalizumab is not advised because her JCV antibody is positive, which raises the risk of PML with longer use; ofatumumab is an equally effective option that she declined in favor of twice-yearly infusions

Before the first infusion: hepatitis B screening (done; not immune), immunoglobulins, varicella and measles immunity, and a pregnancy test; inactivated vaccines at least two weeks before (PCV20, recombinant zoster and hepatitis B started today), and no live vaccines once treatment starts. Check hepatitis B surface antibody one to two months after the series

Re-baseline MRI of the brain three to six months after starting, then yearly; blood count and immunoglobulins before each dose; teach her that infections, especially urinary infections, are more common and can cause a pseudo-relapse that does not need steroids
Occupational therapy for hand function and energy management, and a graded return to practice; aerobic exercise and pacing for fatigue after excluding other causes
